paras: The attempted lynching of W. S. Sims was a failed attempt by an armed band to take Sims, a white physician, from the Aiken County jail in Aiken, South Carolina, on the night of December 5, 1882. Militia ordered out by Governor Thompson guarded the jail, and the band of more than one hundred men turned back without attacking. The case drew notice because of the unnamed charge against Sims, and a week later he was moved to Columbia for safekeeping.

Sims, formerly of Union County, had practiced medicine at Vaucluse and more recently at Langley, and was married to a daughter of the late proprietor of Dorn's Gold Mine in Edgefield County. On his wife's affidavit before Trial Justice R. J. Southall of Langley, he was arrested at Langley on Tuesday, December 5, and committed to jail at Aiken. The South Carolina reports refused to name the charge, calling it a crime "unprovided for by the law," while the Atlanta wire described it as "cruelty to his wife."

According to the New York Herald's correspondent, lynching Sims was "freely discussed in the streets," and Sheriff M. T. Holly, fearing the threats would be carried out, telegraphed the governor for troops. Governor Thompson ordered Captain W. W. Williams to put his Aiken militia company, named variously as the Palmetto Guards, Rifles or Riflemen, at the sheriff's service.

That night, about an hour past midnight by the Herald's account, a band of armed and mounted men marched toward Aiken "for the avowed purpose of lynching Sims." The Aiken correspondents put their number at over one hundred and said they came from Graniteville and Langley. Finding the jail under guard, and urged by some old citizens not to attack because bloodshed would follow, the men went home from the suburbs of the town. A larger party was rumored for the next night, and the jail was guarded again.

No member of the Aiken bar would defend Sims, and a preliminary examination was set for the following Tuesday at Langley. On December 12, after reports that a party was organizing in Edgefield and Augusta to seize him, Judge Aldrich had Sheriff Holly take Sims to the Columbia jail, where Sheriff Rowan held him. There Sims told the sheriff that his treatment was "only the result of political persecution," and friends in Union retained David Johnson to defend him. No report of the examination, an indictment or a trial was found in the coverage.

A Charleston wire of December 6 described the episode in three sentences, naming Sims as "a white man" and a physician, and ran in Washington papers on December 7 and in the Anderson Intelligencer a week later. An Atlanta wire printed in Maine papers on December 8 under "Not Lynched Yet" and "Georgia Lynchers" mislocated the band in its headline, while the Evening Star reprinted the Herald's longer account as "A Doctor's Disgrace."

South Carolina papers were openly sympathetic to the lynchers. The Columbia Register's Aiken letter, reprinted in the Abbeville Press and Banner, ran under a headline calling Sims "the Wretch" and the mob "the Only Tribunal from Which Justice" could be had, though its writer expected no serious trouble. The News and Courier's correspondent wrote that the community was "at fever heat with indignation" but also praised the sheriff's determination, and the Pickens Sentinel called Sims "the brute" whose lynchers were "foiled."

bases: An armed band of over one hundred men marched on the Aiken jail to take and lynch a jailed prisoner and turned back when it found the jail under militia guard (A4, A7, A8).

A band of over one hundred men set out to take Sims from jail and lynch him for a crime he was accused of against his wife, but it turned back and no one was killed (A4, A7, A8); this was an attempted lynching, and the papers identify the intended victim as a white man (A1, A2).

The Charleston wire (A1, A2), the New York Herald account (A4), the Atlanta wire (A5) and separate Aiken letters to the Columbia Register (A7) and the News and Courier (A8) agree on the jailing, the march on the jail and its failure.
